reason: The sources provide rich, verified details across multiple independent sites regarding the capture, geometry, controversy, and legacy of the Pale Blue Dot photograph.
story: On Valentine's Day 1990, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft received a historic set of radio commands nearly 4 billion miles from home. Having completed its planetary flybys, the probe turned its narrow-angle camera back toward the inner solar system before shutting down imaging instruments forever. Over the objections of managers who worried aiming toward the Sun might fry the optics, astronomer Carl Sagan and scientist Carolyn Porco championed taking one final family portrait. Among the 60 frames captured was a single image showing Earth suspended in an accidental beam of scattered sunlight bouncing inside the camera optics. In that frame, our entire world spanned just 0.12 of a single pixel—a tiny speck of blue light containing all of human history, inspiring Sagan's unforgettable reminder that Earth is merely a lonely mote of dust in the cosmic dark.
angle: Earth spans a mere 0.12 of a single pixel, and the dramatic celestial sunbeam illuminating it was actually an optical glare reflecting off the camera's own sunshade.

claims.claim: The Pale Blue Dot photograph of Earth was taken on February 14, 1990.
The image was captured by NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft.
The spacecraft took the photograph from a distance of approximately 4 billion miles (around 6 billion kilometers) from Earth.
Earth's apparent size in the image takes up only 0.12 of a single pixel.
The beam of light across the image was an optical artifact caused by sunlight reflecting off parts of the camera and sunshade.
Astronomer Carl Sagan pushed for years for Voyager 1 to turn around and photograph Earth.
Mission officials long resisted the idea because pointing the cameras toward the Sun risked damaging the sensitive imaging detectors.
Planetary scientist Carolyn Porco independently campaigned for the image and calculated exposure times.
NASA Administrator Richard Truly directly interceded to ensure the photo sequence would be approved and executed.
The photo was part of a 60-frame Family Portrait sequence capturing the Sun and several major planets.
Voyager 1's vantage point when capturing the image was roughly 32 degrees above the ecliptic plane.
Following the acquisition of the Family Portrait images, NASA permanently shut down Voyager 1's camera system to conserve power.
Voyager 1 crossed into interstellar space in August 2012.
Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object in existence.
Carl Sagan featured the image in his 1994 book, famously describing Earth as a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam.
For the image's 30th anniversary in 2020, NASA reprocessed the original data into an updated version named Pale Blue Dot Revisited.
Carolyn Porco later orchestrated a 2013 follow-up image of Earth from Saturn using the Cassini spacecraft, titled The Day the Earth Smiled.
Edward Stone served as the project scientist for the Voyager mission.

disputed: Pixel dimensions: S7 quotes Candy Hansen recalling the dot appearing 'about two pixels big, three pixels big' on her screen when first discovered, whereas formal NASA photometric analysis in S1, S2, and S4 establishes Earth's true size as 0.12 pixel. The script should explain that Earth occupies just 0.12 of a single pixel physically, though displayed raw pixels or point-spread glare may span more on a monitor.

Exact distance measurement: Sources vary slightly between 3.7 billion miles (6.055 billion km / 40.47 AU in S1) and 4 billion miles (6.4 billion km in S4; ~4 billion miles in S2, S3, S5, S6, S7). The script should state 'roughly 4 billion miles' or 'about 6 billion kilometers'.

Year Sagan originally proposed the image: S1 states Sagan proposed the idea in 1980 after the Saturn flyby, while S3 states he submitted his proposal to the project in 1981. The script should say 'in the early 1980s after passing Saturn'.
